title: CDC Issues Level 2 Travel Warning for Costa Rica Over Chikungunya Outbreak
excerpt: The mosquito-borne virus is spreading locally in Costa Rica's popular Guanacaste Province, with India also listed among countries posing elevated risk for US travelers.
body:
• The CDC issued a Level 2 Travel Health Notice for Costa Rica's Guanacaste Province after an outbreak of chikungunya, a mosquito-borne virus that causes severe joint pain lasting months or years.
  • Officials have confirmed 4 cases and identified 17 probable cases in the beach destination of Playa Langosta, with 45 suspected cases investigated in total.
  • India is among 10 countries the CDC lists as posing elevated chikungunya risk for US travelers even without an active outbreak.
  • There is no specific treatment for chikungunya, but a vaccine is available for eligible travelers visiting outbreak areas.

Outbreak in a Popular Tourist Region

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has issued a Level 2 Travel Health Notice — meaning "practice enhanced precautions" — for Costa Rica's Guanacaste Province after a spike in chikungunya cases centered on Playa Langosta, a popular beach destination known for surfing, hiking, and eco-tourism.

Costa Rica's Ministry of Health declared an active outbreak earlier in July after investigating 45 suspected cases in the region. Four have been confirmed and 17 classified as probable, bringing the country's total reported chikungunya cases to 16 in 2026. Both Costa Rican residents and foreign visitors are among those affected.

The CDC noted that the virus is now spreading locally — transmitted by mosquitoes within the community rather than solely imported by travelers — which prompted the elevated advisory. Specialized teams have fumigated approximately 5,000 homes and eliminated mosquito breeding sites in an effort to contain the outbreak.

What Is Chikungunya?

Chikungunya is a viral illness transmitted through bites from Aedes mosquitoes, the same species responsible for spreading dengue and Zika. Symptoms typically appear three to seven days after an infected bite and include high fever, severe joint and muscle pain, headache, joint swelling, and rash.

Most people recover within a week, but some experience debilitating joint pain that persists for months or even years after the acute illness. Newborns, older adults, and people with underlying conditions such as diabetes or heart disease face a higher risk of severe disease, though death from chikungunya is rare.

There is no specific antiviral treatment. A chikungunya vaccine exists and is recommended by the CDC for eligible travelers visiting outbreak areas, though it is not yet widely accessible.

India Among Elevated-Risk Countries

The CDC's chikungunya risk map lists 10 countries where US travelers face elevated risk of exposure even without a declared outbreak. India is among them, alongside Brazil, Colombia, Indonesia, Mexico, Nigeria, Pakistan, Peru, the Philippines, and Thailand.

The designation is based on a median of one or more laboratory-confirmed chikungunya cases reported annually in returning US travelers over the past five years. For Indian Americans planning summer trips to India — particularly to southern and western states where Aedes mosquitoes thrive during the monsoon season — the advisory is a reminder to take mosquito prevention seriously.

India recorded over 90,000 suspected chikungunya cases in 2025, according to the National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control, though actual numbers are likely far higher due to underreporting.

How to Protect Yourself

The CDC recommends several precautions for travelers heading to affected areas:

  • Use EPA-registered insect repellent containing DEET, picaridin, or oil of lemon eucalyptus.
  • Wear long-sleeved shirts and long pants, especially during dawn and dusk when Aedes mosquitoes are most active.
  • Stay in accommodations with air conditioning or window and door screens.
  • Remove standing water around homes or hotel rooms, as mosquitoes breed in stagnant water.
  • Consider vaccination if eligible and traveling to an outbreak area.

The US Embassy in Costa Rica has echoed the CDC guidance and urged travelers to monitor local health advisories. Current active chikungunya outbreaks are also reported in Bolivia, French Guiana, Mauritius, Seychelles, and Suriname.
nri_angle: India is listed among countries posing elevated chikungunya risk for US travelers, and Indian Americans traveling to either Costa Rica or India this summer should take precautions against mosquito bites.
